history.title: George A. Romero Between Night and Dawn (6-Disc Limited Edition) [Blu-ray + DVD] (includes There's Always Vanilla, Season of The Witch and The Crazies)
history.review_title: A Rushed Release, Missing Several Films, Over-priced, From A Company That Should Know Better
history.text: Alright. Arrow is my all-time favorite vendor, followed by Shout/Scream, Warner's Archive Label, Vinegar Syndrome, Code Red, Scorpion and the horribly over-priced Twilight Time label. And, so, for the first time ever, I am going to say something I never thought I would even think in passing: Arrow has gone absolutely crazy. George A. Romero Between Night and Dawn is a 6 disc set retailing for $100 and selling for around $60, a set that contains a whopping THREE movies, none of which are a restoration of Night of the Living Dead. With that, what's worse, Martin, which falls between Night of the Living Dead and Dawn of the Living Dead is NOT even included. I don't know what they were thinking. I don't want to know. This is, simply put, insulting, to us as the fans, to him as the creator, just plain insulting all the way around. This set should have been called From Night to Dawn, retailed for $110, sold for $65 and contained remastered editions of Night of the Living Dead, There's Always Vanilla, Hungry Wives (Season of the Witch), The Crazies, Martin, and a nice copy of Dawn of the Dead, or, if they preferred, $130 selling for $75 and including the remastered multi-version set of Dawn of the Dead they could have licensed from the Zombi release people like me imported last year. The first film is in the public domain. The last film has already had all of the restoration work completed by another company. The intervening films are of a type and from an era that Vinegar Syndrome is routinely able to manage complete remastering, with full clean ups for incredibly low budgets and to a spectacularly high quality results, each and every month of the year. Arrow is better than this. Like crying for Conan The Barbarian, I will be embarrassed for them since they can't seem to be embarrassed for themselves. Here's betting each of these gets an individual release at some point, probably for $15 each on sale, without the extra DVD none of us want, $12 on sale without the extra Blu-ray none of the DVD customers want.

history.title: My Cousin Rachel (2017)
history.review_title: A Nightmare of 30-Second Scenes, No Conversations, Just Snippets and Cuts
history.text: A rarity for me, here I shall review the film, as the film has it coming. To put it bluntly, this is a visually stimulating yet void, vacant, attention-deficit-oriented adaptation of an intricate and nuanced story, with all the intricacies and nuances removed. As an admitted admirer of both Rachel Weisz and Sam Claflin, I was ridiculously excited to hear that they'd been cast in a remake of such a wonderful classic, and as the lead couple. This has been one of my favorite stories and the original was a film I'd longed to see remade, owing to the moral constraints of the time in which it was originally adapted for the screen, not due to any failing on the part of the original players. Knowing their individual talents and tendencies as well as I do, I could imagine precisely how Weisz and Claflin would play certain scenes. And, not surprisingly, they played exactly to expectation, that is to say, in the brief snippets of those scenes this unfortunate director remembered to actually leave in the film. Plainly put, the director has something missing. I don't know what it is, I wish him well if it stems from some health related concern, but, well wishes aside, he has something clearly and tragically missing and, yet, somehow managed to end up writing the script adaptation and directing the film of a story he sadly did not understand. This person becomes so uncomfortable at demonstrations of genuine emotion that, each time his characters find themselves in an emotional situation, he can't seem to cut away fast enough. All of the pivotal scenes conclude in under a minute, most in ten to thirty seconds. Each time the actors attempt to fall into character and engage in meaningful interaction, through dialogue and mutual examination of facial expression and body language, the director seems almost confused by what is happening in front of him and he cuts again. By the time we hit around thirty-seven minutes, if I remember correctly, the game had begun. People viewing with me, adults, in every sense of the word, not drinking, nor prone to misbehavior, began shouting out, at what should have been those beautiful beginning-moments, those origins of two to five minute long conversations between our two leads that tell us everything we need to know about them and color every moment of the film to come, at what were actually entire scenes shot in ten to thirty seconds. And the shouting continued, shouting and exclaiming at a screen which could not hear them, "And he cuts away!", "Here we go again!", "This is madness!" I don't need to tell you that not everyone who began watching the film with me was actually able to finish, as a strange sort of rage swept across the room and people simply began leaving after about seventy minutes. I, sadly, did sit through the entire film and am even more saddened to have to report that this film is not what I would call a film. It plays like a music video, random snippets of facial expressions and dialogue, half-had conversations, single sentences, random moments in time that appear to occur in order but at odd and poorly defined intervals, moments that contain nearly nothing of who the main characters are supposed to be, of how they feel, of what they are to each other. If you have seen My Cousin Rachel, the original, or have read the story, then you know who Rachel and Philip are supposed to be and you can easily fill in the gaps. If you have not seen or read the story, you will most likely walk away from this failing to understand that Rachel is actually meant to be a master manipulator, not cruel, exactly, also not so selfless as she would ask you to believe, and, ultimately, the accidental architect of her fate, such as it is. If you have no experience of him, you might miss that Philip is actually meant to be psychologically disturbed, owing first to having been orphaned and second to his poor upbringing by Ambrose, who had no idea how to raise a child, but also due to a variety of concerns we are meant to figure out for ourselves. And, of course, owing to the fact that it is decidedly British, there is the ever-present issue, the fact that a lack of honest communication is, as it often is, a major player in the story, a fact you can't quite see if every scene stops before it really begins. Issues of money and of independence are at play, the female perspective, the why and how of this woman's choices, even her half-Italian nature, which is ignored in this film entirely with the exception of the label "Italian" having been used, and, most importantly and also most importantly ignored, the issue of sexuality and the use of sex as a weapon by an older, experienced, liberated woman, against a younger, inexperienced, repressed British man-child. And, somehow, most of this is lost in the sea of cuts, lack of conversation, lack of interaction, lack of meaningful communication between the two leads in a story that almost seemed to be crumbling before my eyes, as I watched in deep disappointment. The director almost seems to be making a film exclusively centered on his apparent hobby-horse: female independence, the issue of the day. Apparently honoring some inner monologue of a feminist manifesto, which he probably internalized at some point in his youth, the director seems to be playing out the one-note story of a woman preyed upon by men with no understanding of her situation or the effects of her actions, bounced around, barely coping, seeking only her freedom in a world that tells her to marry and live conventionally, all while he is simultaneously attempting not to insult modern women with the truth of the story. And what is that truth? Going back to the book, this woman over-played her hand and the man's possible madness, in whatever form it takes and from whatever cause, only serves to intensify the man's interpretations of what his cousin deliberately endeavours to lead him to believe. In this film, the woman is merely navigating the difficult waters of a young man's confusion and sexual awakening, having not been married to a British man who certainly would have made her aware of how British men interpret specific actions, particularly sexual actions, taken by women. To be clear, in the book, the woman's confusion, grief, overt-sexuality, inappropriate behavior, coupled with her innocent demeanor, well-wishing and deflection, and possible concealment of guilt, are all clear and vital parts of the text and, here, in spite of the director's obvious intention to avoid them, are all attempted by Weisz. As a professional, she does her level best to convey these many layers, given only seconds on screen for each situation and scene in which she could hope to achieve her desired portrayal. I think she should win the Oscar for doing it as well as she does, in this dud of a film. Still, the director cuts so quickly, so often and so often right in the middle of a scene, even I could feel her performance waning, at times, as though she knew the cut was coming and she couldn't get it all out before the clock ticked down. There were notes of frustration in her performance during particularly short sequences. And, to Claflin. To his credit, he managed to maintain his standard of using his eyes and facial musculature to convey much of what actors must leave unsaid, in the service to the collaborative art-form, but, like Weisz, was, tragically, cut in the most awkward of ways and at the oddest of times. Often just as he made an expression to convey an emotion, the camera quickly reset on a field, candelabra, empty living room, his face at a different time on a different day when he is not feeling quite so much of anything, and so on and so blah. At one point, a pivotal moment, a first kiss, the camera missed much of the scene entirely and fell backward as the director told Weisz to shove Claflin out of the room, using a door, not hands, to achieve it, presumably so as to avoid any of that emotion he seems to find so upsetting. Each time I felt myself drawn in by Claflin or Weisz or both, I knew it was coming, in one or two seconds, the cut away to something else. So pervasive was this terrible direction that, in one scene, a conversation which had been left painfully unfinished, like so many others, had to be continued, awkwardly, for another ten seconds in the next ten-second scene. In the hands of a skilled dramatist, this film might have been more than beautiful to look at. It might have developed, burned that glorious slow-burn we all remember from films past, it might have broken our hearts, disturbed us, left us wanting more. For the first time, ever, I couldn't wait for a visually stunning film, starring people I adore, in a place I love to see, in a style I crave, in a depiction of a story I appreciate to, finally, blessedly, mercifully, end. If you love My Cousin Rachel, watch the other one, read the book, talk about it, dream about it, just don't watch this, please. I never tell people not to watch something, you may have noted from my other reviews, because there is value in everything and we are all so very different. But, watching this can actually take something from you. It won't leave you as you were, only missing a couple of hours, it may actually take a very real part of your appreciation of the story or the original film. In discussing this afterwards, we all felt it, a twinge of disgust at the very idea of viewing the Burton/De Havilland classic. I immediately watched it again, feeling that bit of a, "no, not this", and again, and again, until I felt myself warming to it and returning to a state of love for my old friend, the Black and White masterpiece I had loved for so long. And still, the bliss has not returned and I worry that I may never get the stink of this film out of that clean, bright celluloid jewel from my past. Please, just don't watch this. * For those who read my normal reviews, the Blu-ray is lovely, picture and sound, considering that the film was actually made with muffled, at times garbled, audio. This is the best quality you will get, if you actually find that you want it.

history.title: Harold and Lillian: A Hollywood Love Story [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A Beautiful Love Story, A Beautiful Couple, A Documentary That Isn't Boring. Watch This One.
history.text: This is not my typical Blu-ray review, as I am writing about this film before the disc release. I will update as to picture and sound quality, special features and the like, after it arrives. Today, I am actually reviewing a film because, sadly, no one else has. Generally better reviewers do a wonderful job of explaining film content and I can stick to writing my tech reviews. This is not a normal film. And, with that, here goes.... I don't cry. I was raised by people who survived the Great Depression, two world wars, and horrors like thalidomide, and so was trained, for lack of a better term, not to do so. In trying to figure out how to convey to you, accurately, what this film is, this little documentary, I kept falling on that. Somehow this film made me cry, and I simply don't do that. My uncle was a Broadway actor, never a Hollywood man, even when he moved out here and continued work in theater nearing retirement, never a Hollywood man. His friends were Hollywood people. They would get together and talk, tell their little stories, rather like normal, non-actor people, and the subject of Harold and Lillian Michelson, this couple upon whom everyone depended so completely within the industry, would come up just often enough for me, as the receptacle of the re-told versions, to remember the names, so many years after his death. But I was young and he never told me all of the stories, just the highlights. So, when I noticed this film, a documentary about the life, married and working, of this legendary Hollywood couple, I thought I'd finally familiarize myself with who these people were, these people everyone kept talking about, off handed, in discussing something they were working on, something they needed done, something they'd achieved about which they'd felt particularly good. And I sat down to view what can only be described as one of the most beautiful and most honestly presented love stories I have ever seen. In a world where Ron Howard invented a new, more palatable, lovable version of John Nash, at times dispensing with reality altogether, in an effort to craft some perfect love story, here is a film that tells the story as it was, with a practical dedication to truth, accuracy, getting it right, because this couple was so special, in an industry that eats marriages, and their story was so inspiring, that to alter it in any way would have cheapened it. Harold and Lillian Michelson were a husband and wife team who never really set out to work as a team, and of course worked independently as well. Harold was a storyboard artist, the guy who designed the visuals of the film from the ground up and then passed his visuals off to directors who used them as a start point in filming every scene of a film. He advanced, of course, as one of the most talented the industry ever saw, and ended up a production designer, the person responsible for making something on screen appear, to us as the audience, to be real and to fit when, oftentimes, the objects and spaces we are viewing don't look like what we see on screen. He was the guy who made the engine in Star Trek The Motion Picture look like this incredibly long and large thing. It had been build in forced perspective and was actually pretty small. I remembered that, from my youth, the story of the production designer for Star Trek The Motion Picture and what he achieved, at a time when I truly didn't care about such things, and how he was nominated for but lost the Oscar, a fact which angers me to this day, a thing he found to be a relief. Lillian was a researcher, working in a library and handling everything from the basics of how people lived in certain parts of the world to how they dressed, talked, what they believed in, in subcultures within American cities and in historical periods about which a film was to be made. She was, pardon the expression, the human Internet, for you young people and was actually replaced by the Internet at the dawn of the new Millennium. She maintained and expanded upon a seemingly endless collection of information from which everyone who needed information could draw. She got people in the FBI and the CIA to tell her how things worked, like drug trafficking and blowing up buildings, so that filmmakers could make their stories seem real. Oddly, Criminologist me, didn't care about those ones. It was her dramas, whether in a horror film or science fiction or just a regular old planet Earth-based slice of life, it was her unparalleled ability to give people exactly what they needed in order to make a film real, so real that it became uncomfortable. That was what most impressed me. Her grand achievement, in an era of no Internet, was to give people like Roman Polanski everything they needed to know about to make Rosemary's Baby, Alfred Hitchcock everything he needed to know about safes and banks and horses and hounds and bays and gasoline and birds in order to make Marnie and The Birds (with Harold on the Hitchcock films as well). Together, oftentimes, this couple turned films that, otherwise, would have been drab and fake and felt unimportant, into masterpieces. They worked on everything, their hands in every pie. If you've seen a film from the sixties or eighties and thought "that was incredible, beautiful, felt really real", it was probably one of theirs. They did Star Trek together, Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf, The Graduate.... They did Hollywood together, the whole experience, the working, the living, the raising a family. This film managed, without boring me, anti-documentary person that I am, to tell me who these people were. From how they met, how they lived, him as a flier in WWII, her in orphanages escaping into books, to their move to Los Angeles, his struggle to find work, her time supporting the family, their kids, one of whom was autistic in a time when that word was not used and the syndrome was not understood, to his accident and subsequent pain and prolonged recovery period with a leg that wouldn't heal and crippling depression, struggles in their marriage, their lives, their jobs, all the way through to a marriage that lasted for sixty years. How do you sum up the story of a couple's life, a couple that actually put in the work and the time and loved each other enough to make it, when they didn't have to, when they could have split up at any point along the way. I don't know how. I just watched this for the third time and I have no idea how the team behind this managed to put it all together, the interviews, the storyboards, film clips, archival footage, all of it, into a cohesive whole, such that I feel like I just watched an old Hollywood drama about a family, a couple and their evolution over a half of a century. Really, there is only one thing to say, beyond the basics of who this couple was in the industry, what they did, so you know what you'll be watching, and that is, simply put, that listening to Lillian Michelson tell the story of her marriage made me cry. I hope you watch this, whoever you are. It applies. Update: The picture quality on this is wonderful, with bright colors, even on the cleaned-up archival footage necessary to make a documentary like this, which was surprising. There is nice clarity on the fine details and the image is pleasing, which is what I look for. The sound is better than the presentation I had seen previously, with solid stability, no surprise changes in volume at odd moments, a clear voice track that allows ease of understanding, regardless of who is speaking. This is an excellent presentation of a fine film so, if you can get it on Blu-ray, that is the way to go.

history.title: Cary Grant Film Collection
history.review_title: Great Films, Packaged Poorly, In A Disaster Of A Scratchy Cardboard Case
history.text: I have bought six of this and returned five, three here at Amazon with one of those being the one that I settled on. Here is the problem, and it is a big one. The case design is a cardboard slip case where discs slide down into little slots for safe keeping. The cardboard is not slick enough, nor safe enough, for the disc surfaces and, as such, the discs are all scratched and, furthermore, scratched to an extreme degree. In one set, every disc was scratched so heavily over so much of the surface that I didn't even bother testing them. The one I kept, the best of six, has scratches on each disc, of course, but the scratching is only heavy on two discs and is lighter and more spread out on the other four. Be aware of the issues with this set and the highly variable quality on it when you purchase and make sure to check your discs carefully. Good luck with this one.

history.title: The Vampire Diaries: Season 6 [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Defective Case Issue On The Season Six Blu-Ray Only
history.text: I am not reviewing the content except to say that I love The Vampire Diaries. A friend wanted the series on Blu-ray and was missing certain sets so I went about getting it for her, and got a set for myself as well. With Season Six, there is a case issue. Not all cases will be broken but I ended up buying four of this, three from sellers here and one at Best Buy in person, all four cases were broken. The plastic was noticeably thinner than the plastic for the mega-sets on Seasons Three, Four and Five but also different from the plastic on One and Two, so that may be the reason. A weaker, thinner case for only a few discs, as compared to the odd sets they made for the sets of Blu-rays combined with DVDs, would explain such breakage and eco measures to thin out the plastic, thereby using less of it to make each case, would appear to explain the difference from the early sets. Seasons Seven and Eight were fine, thicker plastic. I ended up returning all but the used one I bought for myself and then got her a gift card to get herself this season, so she could decide how to handle it. As for how to deal with it, they sell individual cases for these sets all over the place so, I'll get to the point finally, if you are buying this and get a broken case that is not too terrible, just keep it as many are broken and some are just terribly cracked and chipped and basically falling apart. What you exchange it for will likely be worse, on Season Six only. If you get a really bad one, you can exchange or return for a slightly damaged case or the elusive intact case, you can opt to buy a replacement case for five dollars or so, from a random vendor, or of course you have the option to just deal with that case. Essentially, this review is a warning that if you are purchasing this particular season as a gift, on the clock as it were, then you should leave enough time to exchange it or to purchase a replacement case before you need to to pass it on to the recipient. Again, this is an isolated issue with the Season Six set of The Vampire Diaries on Blu-ray. All other seasons appear to be made of slightly thicker plastic. Good luck finding what is right for you and, in case you are just reading reviews to decide on whether to get this, like all of The Vampire Diaries, it is a wild, fun and dramatic ride that is absolutely worth taking, if you love vampire stories and lots of beautiful men kissing lots of beautiful women. Enjoy.

history.title: The Crown Platinum Edition Gift Set [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A Beautiful Show. A Terrible Gift Set.
history.text: I hate to say it, as the first season of The Crown was spectacular, however, this gift set leaves much to be desired. First, there is the failure to include an Ultraviolet (UV or HD Digital) copy with the set. Given the current standard for nearly all releases of all shows and films, that a code for the digital version is included for viewing on devices from anywhere so that a set can be left at home, the lack of a code was an unpleasant surprise. Second, there are no deleted scenes, no interviews, not even the standard making of featurette that you would find on the worst film of the year, let alone on a complete series set. Third, and of greatest importance in our home, it was believed by the purchaser, not me, that he would be getting a book with the set. Actually, the set includes a little booklet, not a commemorative booklet for the series, but a little booklet containing the first chapter, and only the first chapter, of a much larger and longer book you would have to purchase separately if you wanted it. Essentially, this is not a gift set. It is the same bare bones release you can purchase for far less money only it has been repackaged in a bloated cardboard case with advertising material (the first chapter of the book they didn't include) with a tiny coin, that would be rather difficult to display in your home and would get lost if not kept in the case at all times, stuck in the box for good measure, and no special features whatsoever. My family was disappointed but, since he got it for the same price as the regular release, I wasn't upset that he bought it. The gift sets usually sold for shows like Outlander, as one example, contain a great deal of pictorial and prop related material, like a commemorative book in one set, pictures, photographs, one set even had a flask, and of course the Digital copy. This isn't even a gift set. It is the packaging for a gift set with the gifts left out. Good luck in finding what you are looking for. Sorry to burst your bubble on this but it is a lot of money to spend on a whole lot of smoke and mirrors. If you want this set, there is a standard release without the packaging and space that should have been filled with the kinds of things one would expect in a gift set.

history.review_title: This "FILM" is NOT A FILM. This is ONE HALF of a film. BE WARNED
history.text: For clarity, for anyone who isn't aware, this is NOT A COMPLETE FILM. The people over at Lifetime thought it would be a great idea to make a film telling the first half of a story and then finish it up in a book. This "film" comprises approximately one half of the "Thornwood Heights" story, unfortunately, the first half, and the second appears only in the book "When Secrets Kill", with select pieces of information only available on the interactive website. This kind of multi-platform, attention-deficit marketing is typically reserved for children and teens, with the recent one-off resurrection of NBC's Heroes springing to mind. If you recall, NBC thought that assigning homework would be a great way to net viewers, with much of the story taking place in alternate platforms, comics and videos online and possibly a video game. The resulting television show dragged and left people wondering why they hadn't just put all their eggs in one nicely packaged TV basket instead of splitting them up and throwing them at the wall. I also remember tuning into a series, marketed as an action and sci-fi blend, Defiance, if memory serves, in which all of the action actually took place in an online video game which had a story paralleling the so-called story in the show. I forced myself to watch a season and still wish I could undo it. And so, back to the big Lifetime/Harlequin whatchamacallit, we have seen many successful Harlequin stories turned into successful and even beloved Lifetime film adaptations. This marks the first time we are seeing half a story thrown willy-nilly at the screen with no closure and no consideration for those of us who wanted to watch a Lifetime film, film being that thing where you sit down and passively view a collaborative video and audio presentation designed to, passively, deliver unto you an ENTIRE STORY, in under two hours. It is the first time we are seeing the back half of said story getting written down, sold separately, never to be delivered in film format, not to be completed in under two hours, not so much a nice temporary escape from life but an assignment to read a book we wouldn't have read because we would have been reading something else, sadly, something better. I imagine many of the actors on this project wrapped filming and felt very confused. And so, don't watch this unless you really want to sit down and read a book immediately afterwards and spend some time on a website. It was so unsatisfying, especially given how many stellar and underutilized actors showed up in it, that I had to run off and watch Nora Roberts' Tribute to clean off the ick. Who doesn't love Lewis and Murphy. Had she lived, she would have made many more wonderful films and here's betting every single one would have HAD AN ENDING. I hate telling people not to.... "Don't go to Vegas with your buddy, he's just gonna get you drunk and take you to a strip club" and "Don't eat that, you'll end up looking like me." However, in this case, I give you fair warning and an apology, I am sorry to have to break it to you, but, this film, this should-have-been-great, with a great story and all the actors you love to watch (Penikett is in it for crying out loud) "FILM", is NOT A "FILM" at all. It is a half of a film. There are currently no plans to film the other half. Lifetime apparently hates you, and me, and everyone else who has remained a loyal and dedicated fan for, oh, let's say, since we were young and beautiful and unmarried. This actually really irritated me and I hope to spare you the same outcome. Good luck finding a film that suits you. After writing this, I think I'll go Nora Roberts again. Amazon has those films, FYI.

history.review_title: Amazon Video Transfer NOT the SAME as on the DVD
history.text: This is not a review for content, as you either enjoy this version of Marple or you don't. This is a review of picture / sound or, if you prefer, video and audio quality. Acorn, the official distributor of Marple in America is responsible for the streaming video here and, for no reason I can fathom, have completely dropped the ball. As a fan of Marple, all Marple, I have seen this many times in many formats. From original airings to the Region 1 / NTSC / USA DVD release to the Blu-ray release in Spain and HD streaming from Netflix and Hulu, I have watched every version of this. I purchased these episodes because I put them on so often it was getting annoying putting the Blu-ray in over and over. It was a waste of money. This video and audio is the lowest quality I have seen. The sound is somewhat muddled and muted and has too much bass. It has to be turned up to hear dialogue properly but, when turning it up, the bass gets even louder. The video is a TV tragedy. This is available in HD transfer so why they chose SD is beyond me. However, SD can and often does look very good on a quality, upscaling HD television set. That is not the case with this transfer. Where the DVDs, from Acorn, look fairly good, with vibrant colors, though not as bright as on Blu-ray, and an excellent absence of odd pixellation, this video is fuzzy, pixellates often (not from any streaming issue, as it happens in the same places each viewing) and the colors are muted even as compared to the DVD. The best example of this color issue is Miss Marple herself. Her clothing and the redness in the tissue of her inner eyelids are all the wrong color, throughout. Acorn, again, for whatever reason, just didn't bother with a decent transfer and, though they are passing this off as the official Acorn version, it is clearly not the same digital transfer as from their own DVD. Wherever the Netflix and Hulu HD versions came from, from what I could tell, identical to the Region B Blu-ray, is the transfer that is worth viewing. My recommendation, for what it's worth, is to purchase a used DVD or, if you have a Region free player, get the Blu-ray. Don't pay Acorn for their failure to care about the needs of their audience. They didn't bother doing a proper job on this one and it really shows. Good luck finding what works best for you.

history.review_title: The Same Transfer As On The DVD Set, Solid Video And Audio
history.text: This is an Amazon Video specific review. I am not here to review the content of Ellery Queen, as you can find wonderful reviews all over the place covering all of the subjective issues like actors and set design from people who are very passionate about such things. I am very passionate about picture and sound, the good old fashioned video and audio quality battle, from one transfer to the next, who wins. First, there is no Blu-ray of Ellery Queen anywhere in the world. I would know. There is an excellent DVD release that was discontinued and costs quite a lot of money, more than most have to spend, even on an old favorite like this. I happen to have the DVD, from when it was much less expensive, have watched it many times, and will again. But, when I am being lazy and want some Ellery, right now, no effort put forth, I turn on Amazon Instant Video and watch an episode. And so, in comparison, I have found that the DVD transfer source and the Amazon Video transfer source are, indeed, the same, identical, original source material. Considering the type of limited restorative work that was done for the DVD, the film actually cleaned up quite well and looked pretty clean, with good color and image stability, for a DVD. I really believe that with a little love they could manage an HD transfer but, truly, that is never going to happen and we are lucky they took this digital transfer while the celluloid was still in good condition. Of course that is the DVD. Lucky for you, if you are reading this, the Amazon Video is the same, with the same little flaws here and there, and I do mean little, the same great picture quality, stability and color, with that classic half-moon nightmare orange sofa in the pilot film to prove it. The picture is, like the DVD, clean and, for the most part, stable, as said, and the color reflects what I remember of Ellery's study, Dad's office, and the various New York staples we see throughout. The audio is also the same, that is to say that it is also identical to the DVD set, and quite good considering the source. I know it matters to no one but, if they could find a way to do the same for McMillan & Wife, similar in quality on DVD to the Ellery Queen DVDs, that would be a spectacular Amazon Video find. But, back to Ellery, I highly recommend the Amazon Video version of the first season, when it is under thirty dollars, to anyone who cannot afford one of the remaining DVD sets. It looks as good as it likely ever will and sounds better than I remember, because my television is better, as are all of yours. I think that huge monstrosity is still disassembled in a huge box out in the garage. Good luck finding what you are looking for.

history.title: The Amicus Collection [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Delayed Release Due To Error On Cases, Severin Has Fixed It And They're Shipping
history.text: Update: The new cases are wonderful and fit perfectly. The Collection is shipping out. Mine arrived on release day, January 16th, and they are already shipping out the high numbers. So, get your Limited Edition while they have it, if you are wanting one of the 3500 they're making of this fantastic set. True, I'm still miffed at the terrible job Severin did on their "restoration" of The Baby, where they somehow forgot that open matte full frame for a TV director is the correct aspect ratio, such that cutting off the top and bottom of the frame cuts valuable visual cues and acting, and spaced out on the color correction, as it is not supposed to make film look like it has been stored in a garage, but so far these films, Asylum, And Now The Screaming Starts, The Beast Must Die, plus the bonus disc, The Vault Of Amicus, are looking AWESOME. Yes, I intended that as a yell, or, rather, more of a girly shriek. If you love these films, go for it. Screen grabs are already up on mondo-digital because they are so good at what they do, so feel free to check those before ordering if you are on the fence, and those caps are accurate to what I am seeing on my set. This is the best these films will ever look and, for the record, they do look really good, better than I thought they would by a large margin given the previous versions I'd seen but also given The Baby. Well, this is no repeat of The Baby. They got it right this time. The sound is great, and I'm picky, especially when it comes to Hammer favorites like Peter Cushing. I can't recommend this highly enough, even with the little bit of a white band down the very edge of one film, noticeable in places but I forgot about it quickly as, again, the transfer looks so great, even on that one. I'm gushing so I'll shut up now and get back to watching. Thank you Severin, for the work you all put in on this. Original Review Information: Just a heads up, for anyone checking here to see if others have received their sets, The Amicus Collection from Severin, though listed here as "temporarily out of stock", implying it has previously been in stock, was delayed by an unfortunate error at the print shop that made the cardboard cases. The issue has been dealt with and the company is proceeding with assembly of the sets at a quick but careful pace. These will be in soon, at Severin and at Amazon, but not for December 19th, clearly. As the price is so good, if you purchased this as a gift, I advise printing out a picture of the set from the Severin website and wrapping up a nice card with the photo. If they are a fan, they'll know what it is and won't mind waiting. If you are like me, and you saved up to buy this for yourself, then you are probably also like me in knowing that a quality set, like this one, is worth the wait, as perfection always is. Good luck.

history.title: Pixels [DVD]
history.text: Silly, grade-school humor. Not for adults. Poor logic to justify the attack. Unrealistic relationships. Not very funny. After ten minutes, I pulled the DVD out and gave it away. I'm 82 and lived through the gaming era with nine grand kids, who really could play these games. (Lots of quarters, finally PC versions.) Just to put my opinion in perspective, I'm a Bond, Star Wars, Star Trek and Bourne fan, who owned all the movies starting with VHS. Of course now I have them all on BD and 3D BD.

history.title: X-MEN: APOCALYPSE
history.text: Excellent CG, sound, directing by Brian Singer, acting, editing, HOWEVER, in my opinion, a really silly movie. Every plot point a cliche, been there, done that, seen that, over and over again! Nothing new, no matter how skillfully done, sorta boring.

history.title: The Accountant (DVD)

history.title: Peter Pan - Starring Mary Martin
history.text: When Captain Hook Intends to poison Peter, but poisons Tinkerbell, Peter asks children "Do you believe in fairies? This is faith in humanity. Though the years that faith has been tested, through "Peter Pan Live!" (which I reviewed) though the Election of Donald Trump, which made me feel the same way that "Peter Pan Live!" did, as the Ringling Brothers And Barnum and Bailey Circus draws to a close. As an adult, it's hard to believe on fairies, especially when you see how horrible humanity can be. But you must believe! Especially if you believe in youth, joy, and freedom for all. I LOVED the fact that Mary Martin was a women, because I was a six-year-old girl. The Musical defined me as a Feminist, even if I was too young to know what Feminism was. "Peter Pan Live!" took the two most powerful women in my universe, the women that played Peter Pan, and Tiger Lily, and SEXUALIZED them! NBC's power-trip of changing "Ugg-A-Wugg" because it was racist, was a miserable, and isolating experience. How could they claim not to be racist, and then, sexualize Native American women through Tiger Lily? The song is still followed by "Distant Melody" and the lyrics became PAINFULLY RELEVANT. The saving grace of "Peter Pan Live" was "When I went Home" the song that Peter sings about feeling abandoned and betrayed. It was no surprise that this was the song cut from the Original Broadway Production, It sounded like it was from the writers whose Musical I loved. Their last gift to me was making it ok to cry. I was sad, because up until that point I HAD believed in fairies, and that Mary Martin, my role model, had never done anything wrong. Plus NBC had done "Peter Pan" with Mary Martin, and a fair number of children, and had denounced them as racist. Social Justice Warrior that I am, I think the media could have handled it better. Like copying and pasting the Lyrics to "Ugg-A-Wugg" INSTEAD of posting videos with children in them. and NOT saying "Ugg-A-Wugg" was meaningless simply because you can't understand them. As a person with a disability, people can't understand me a lot, and at the time I first saw "Peter Pan" I was in speech therapy, so when the tape would come to "Ugg-A-Wugg" I would watch the brilliant Jerome Robbins choreography, and I would listen. I came to the conclusion that it meant "help" except "Ugg-Ugg-Wah" which meant "I Promise." ( Ableism is more of an undertone in this conversation) That "I Promise" was powerful, because with it I swore my loyalty to the characters, and the cast. When the lyrics were changed and NBC broke their loyal bonds by saying that everyone who worked on, or loved "Peter Pan" is o horrible racist, Sondra Lee, came to my rescue like she promised, just by giving an interview saying how sad she was, because she had happy memories off "Peter Pan" just like I did. The happiness it brought me was nothing to feel ashamed of, Sondra Lee is the hero of this story for relieving my isolation just enough, so I could watch "Peter Pan Live!" so I could tell people NBC is an EVIL HYPOCRIT! No, I couldn't be a Social Justice Warrior if I didn't believe in Fairies.
