history.title: Spider-Man: Homecoming [Blu-ray] [3D Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Lots of fun, but nothing new
history.text: Spider-Man's back! Surely that's a statement that should have people much more excited, but after Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2 the film franchise has gone on a steep decline. This is the second reboot of the web-swinger's motion picture adventures in less than a decade, and people are a bit tired because the quality of the latests films has ranged from mediocre to terrible. Does this movie return the franchise to enjoyable levels? Most definitely, just like The Force Awakens did for Star Wars. But just like that film, this one plays it too safe for its own good. Let's go over the positives first. Avoiding the pitfalls of The Amazing Spider-Man, this movie doesn't retread Sam Raimi's original film. Nor is an origin story in any capacity. This is good, because since this movie is set in the MCU alongside Iron Man, Dr. Strange and Thor all those superhero origin stories are starting to look the same. It's also a much more personal story rather than the last two films dealing with city-wide threats. In that respect it's a bit of fresh air. Then there's the whole deal with Spider-Man's suit being made by Tony Stark (aka Iron Man), which entails Peter Parker learning to use foreign tech he's not prepared to handle. The way the movie deals with Peter Parker is also really good. They show him having to juggle all his superhero responsibilities, highschool work and personal life stuff. It's also the first time where Peter Parker is correctly represented as a teenager, who looks and behaves like one. The villain is very well represented and wonderfully portrayed. On to the negatives, I feel like this movie doesn't really do anything special. There are a couple of surprising moments here and there but in general this feels more like a long episode of a TV series with more production values. The script just doesn't like to take risks. And while the movie handles Peter well, it doesn't do so great with Spidey. The fact that Spider-Man's suit has so much tech makes it feel less like Spider-Man and more like Iron Man Jr. And there's a problem from this film showing up so late in the MCU's life. Spider-Man used to stand out in Marvel comics for being a wise-cracker. But since pretty much every hero in the MCU is a jokester now, loving that ironic humor and sarcasm, Spidey feels like just another guy. It's one of the things that contributes to the film's generic feeling. The worst problem is Spider-Man's motivation. Yeah, it's great that they don't show us yet again Uncle Ben dying and all that, but that doesn't mean they should just remove the motivation. Spider-Man has always been about responsibility. Here, Spidey's entire motivation is to impress Tony Stark. Not only it makes it look less heroic, but also makes this move less about him. Tony Stark's physical presence in the film is short, but his influence spreads throughout the whole movie. Hell, even the villain is yet again a guy with a grudge against Stark (as if we didn't have enough of those in the Iron Man and Avengers movies). And I get that introducing diversity in films is a good thing, but could we please at least try to make it a bit realistic? One look at Peter Parker's group of friends and you'll expect them at any time to take out their rings and call Captain Planet. They look like a fast food chain commercial rather than a realistic group of friends. There's also a bit of excess humor. There are some genuinely funny moments, but others are predictable and annoying. I'd rather have quality over quantity. Now, make no mistake, the movie is a lot of fun, but there's nothing in it that will stay in you for days or even years after watching it. If you allow me to use a crude remark, this movie is like cranking one out: yeah, it's a fun way to pass the time, but it's not particularly memorable. Hopefully the next film in the franchise is able to shed away the fear of rejection and do its own thing.

history.title: DCU: Batman and Harley Quinn (BD)
history.text: Harley Quinn's popularity has risen well enough over the last few years that DC has put her everywhere to the point of annoyance, just like they did with, well, Batman. Considering this, it's strange that it took until this moment to make a movie in which they share title credit. Shame for Nightwing, though, who has a role just as large as any of them both yet the title completely ignores. Then again, after watching the film, maybe he asked his agent not to put this one on the résumé. As much as I believe both Batman and Harley Quinn are overused, I love both characters, so a movie about them was instantly interesting. The trailers did nothing for me, but they didn't look terrible, just uninteresting. Sadly, they turned out to be much more telling than I thought, because that's probably the best way to describe this movie: "not terrible, just uninteresting". Your mileage might vary, though. If you hate this movie, I'll understand. The obvious appeal of this film is the visual aspect, using the same art style from the classic DCAU Batman series, and some of the same voice cast. The movie doesn't explicitly state that it occurs in the same continuity (and if it does, there are a couple of continuity problems with it), but on the surface it looks like an extended episode of the series. Kevin Conroy and Loren Lester are back as Batman and Nightwing, and for them these roles are like putting back a comfortable pair of pajama pants. They slip in effortlessly. Less lucky is Melissa Rauch (who you might know as Bernadette from The Big Bang Theory) as Harley Quinn. While Rauch has a natural voice that fits the character perfectly, here she's instead trying an imitation of original voice actress Arleen Sorkin, which feels terribly forced and sounds excruciatingly grating. The plot is as follows: Batman foe Poison Ivy teams up with similarly plant-themed creature and relatively obscure DC villain the Floronic Man in order to find the formula that transformed scientist Alec Holland into similarly plant-themed less-obscure-but-still-not-very-famous DC "hero" Swamp Thing, and use it to transform all of Earth's living beings into plant life. Batman is forced to recruit the help of Ivy's friend Harley Quinn in order to locate her before she can put her plan into action. Hijinks ensue. If you're a fan of the Batman animated series this movie is based on, you'll recognize that this is pretty much the exact same plot as the one from episode "Harlequinade" (Season 2, Episode 7), only replacing Joker with Ivy and adding Nightwing for good measure, so no points for originality. The way the story develops is less than ideal as well, with too many unnecessary, long scenes added just for the sake of a joke or two. The padding is obvious, and it's clear that the plot of a 22-min episode it's not enough to fill a 74-min movie. Worse, while this movie (seemingly) forms part of the DCAU, it expects you to have extensive knowledge about characters that have never been introduced in it until now. If you happen, for instance, to know nothing about Swamp Thing coming here, prepare to be swamped (tee hee). But fine, you can claim that the story is merely an excuse to get these characters together. How do they fare? Not very well, I say. While at moments the characters feel well like themselves, more than once they simply change personality in order to make others look different or just for (again) the sake of a joke. If you've ever seen a Michael Bay movie you'll know what I'm talking about. Characters just don't feel cohesive enough. And let's not even get to the ending scene, which is an exercise in insulting both the audience and the characters. Which brings me to the worst part: the humor. Now, the Batman animated series (and the entire DCAU in general) had a great handling on humor. The writers made sure it fit. You wouldn't have Batman cracking a joke about sexy girls just like you wouldn't have Flash pretending to threaten a criminal with a deadly disease only to reveal it was just water all along. The humor in this movie is TERRIBLE. It's Adam Sandler quality. Did you expect to live your whole life knowing that there'd never be a Batman movie with fart jokes? Well, I'm sorry to inform you that even if you die tomorrow, that ship has already sailed. From the very beginning, the Pink-Panther-movie-like intro credits are a massive red flag but trust me, you won't be prepared for just how bad it gets. All in all, I can't recommend this movie, unless maybe you're a diehard fand of the Floronic Man, who's the only character that doesn't get thoroughly trashed. It gets points for Bruce Timm's classic visual style, most of the voice acting and some of the action scenes, but the rest is uninteresting at best and rage-inducing at worst. Unexplicably, the writer for this movie, James Krieg, has worked in the excellent Green Lantern animated series, Batman: the Brave and the Bold and 90's Spider-Man animated series. He can clearly craft a good story, so I don't know what happened. Executive meddling would be my guess. "Make it more kid-friendly" (which it most certainly isn't, by the way), "Make it funnier", "Do this", "Do that". Just another victim of someone with lots of power and zero talent overtaking those in the opposite position. A shame.

I never watched the previous live-action incarnation of The Tick. I've only sporadically taken a look at the cartoon and I've sampled very few of the comics, but I understand what The Tick is about. It has been ingrained in me like Star Trek, The Godfather or other movies or shows that I've only watched long after pop culture made them familiar to me, despite its relative obscurity. That's why I wasn't enthusiastic by the trailer. It looked like it couldn't decide on a tone, and the humor (very important for the character) seemed lacking. I still decided to watch the pilot, and I'm glad I did, because I was instantly hooked. While not as over-the-top ridiculous as previous incarnations, this series takes a slightly more realistic approach (or rather, sticks the title character in a somewhat realistic world), but the series doesn't suffer for it. In fact, it's probably one of its biggest strengths, as it help us relate all the more to the main character, as he finds himself suddenly thrust into insanity. The real protagonist of the series is Arthur, a mild-mannered guy who suffers from PTSD after witnessing the death of his father and favorite team of superheroes at the hand of supervillain The Terror. The world believes The Terror is dead, killed at the hand of major superhero Superian, but Arthur knows better and he's determined to prove it, well against the wishes of his protective sister. In the middle of investigating criminal smuggling a technological powersuit, he's suddenly made the target of a friendly stalking by an unknown and outlandish superhero called The Tick, who's determined to prove Arthur that his destiny is to become a hero. Finding himself unwillingly wearing the suit, Arthur is now the target of the criminal organization and needs to figure out if he wants to come back to his old complicated but familiar life or embrace the call of heroism. While Arthur is the protagonist, the titular character is the star. The Tick is sane but wacky, strange but heroic and annoying but well-intentioned. While he never reachs camera-winking levels of 4th-wall breaking like, say, Deadpool does, he's a bit self-referential and seemingly more aware of the rules of storytelling than about his own existence. He really is a lot of fun, but a lot of his humor depends on context and that's likely to be the reason why the trailer didn't interest me. All of the characters are great and wonderfully portrayed, but the main two easily steal the show, The Tick with his wackiness and Arthur with his emotional backstory. This is a series that deserves to go on for longer, and I hope it does, because I want more of it.

history.title: Arrow: The Complete Fifth Season [Blu-ray]
history.text: Seasons 3 and 4 of Arrow were pretty divisive. Even those who liked them had to admit there were aspects of them that didn't fit together and as a result there was a lot of disjointed episodes and both seasons suffered from characterization issues. The showrunners realized they had to do something if they intended to win the audience back, and they did: it's called Arrow Season 5. A real back to form for the series, it's just as good as the first two seasons. Oliver Queen is the new mayor of Star City, and now has to reconcile these responsibilities with his night job as the Green Arrow. The events of the last season have made him wonder if he did the wrong thing by taking a non-lethal approach to crime fighting, and this decision coupled with personal issues and responsibilities from other members of his team have caused a split up. Now Oliver finds himself training a new team to fight crime while a new crime boss is taking the place of the last one. Meanwhile, a new villain peeks on the horizon. Someone with a personal grudge against the Green Arrow and working in the shadows to test Oliver like he's never been tested before. It's important to mention that the major problem with the last two seasons was the relationship plot tumor. The writing seemed more focused on finding new ways to make Oliver have relationship issues than in advancing the plot, and both the story and characters suffered in consequence. A secondary problem was that the classic flashback subplots were stretched far beyond need, spending several episodes to solve something that should take only one. Both of these were corrected in this season. Relationships now don't take focus away from the plot, characters are not forced to behave in ridiculous ways just to create conflict and the flashbacks are well crafted. Acting is better than ever. In particular Stephen Amell does his best work to date and the villain is simply astonishing. The story is well crafted as well, and leaving aside a couple of episodes that deal with personal issues or a crossover between all DC CW shows, the plot advances with good pacing. If next season is half as good as this one it'll still be great. A note aside, because I see some silly reviews complaining: yes, there's an episode dealing with gun control. But no, it's not propaganda from whatever side. It presents the issue as one that's not easily solved and doesn't really take any sides. Ignore the ramblers, the show is here to tell a story, not to sell political propaganda.

history.title: The Flash: The Complete Third Season [Blu-ray]
history.text: A spin-off from Arrow, The Flash started out with a spectacular first season that raised the stakes for superhero TV shows. Second season was just as good for most of its running time, faltering a bit at the end (including a severe drop in writing quality in a particular episode). Hopes were still high for third season, Seeing how those few quality drops were the exception and not the rule. Sadly, they seem to be the new rule. It's not a bad show by any means, but it feels like going back to the "Lois and Clark " time. A time where continuity wasn't a priority and characters would act as the plot demanded rather than how their personalities did. That worked back then, but in 2017 this is not one, but several steps back. The consequences of Season 2's finale left Barry Allen in a bad emotional shape. Not being able to stand the pain, Barry traveled back in time to stop his mother's death (the event that kickstarted his careers as both a forensic investigator and The Flash), creating a new life for himself. Taking cues from the event that inspired this season's plotline, "Flashpoint", Barry finds himself dealing with the consequences of his meddling with the timeline slowly robbing him of his powers and memories. While he manages to "repair" the timeline, cracks start to show up and Barry realizes he's now created a new enemy for himself, a speedster named Savitar, who has a personal crused against Barry and intends to ruin his life. Time travel is always a complicated subject, and rules are hard to keep track of. Even in the first two seasons of this show, the rules have been shaky, but it was forgiven because the writing was good. But here, the complete and utter lack of respect for continuity reaches frustrating levels. The entire arc of the season only starts because writers ignore the rules established by the previous two and then proceed to further mangle them well beyond recognition. For instance, Barry has an ally from a parallel universe who has to hide his face due to his version in this universe being a known criminal, and at some point he's found giving a public lecture with his face well on display on several pictures, and no explanation is offered as to why people forgot this guy's a wanted criminal. But even when not dealing with time travel the writing is poor quality. The plot only happens because everyone acts like a fool. Heroes seem unable to learn their lessons and keep comitting the same mistakes. Characterization comes and goes. Some characters are not given their due and others are given too much despite not needing it. Some adaptations of popular villains from the comics are devoid from all what makes them interesting. But the worst part, without any shadow of a doubt, is the main villain of the season. He's boring, uninteresting, and visually unappealing. It's only in the last few episodes when they inject a little characterization on him, yet he never even reaches the level of one-note monster-of-the-week, despite being a season-spanning villain. It says a lot when the most interesting villain of this season is actually the major antagonist on another show. Make no mistake, it's still a fun show. It has its touches of good writing, nice action scenes and the acting ranges from adequate to great (particularly Tom Cavannagh, who's just as exceptional here as he was in the previous two seasons). The problem is that the issues are so prominent that they keep preventing you from partaking in that fun. Here's hoping the show doesn't have to wait until its fifth season to come back to its greatness like Arrow did.

history.title: Transformers: The Last Knight
history.review_title: An instant classi... HAHAHA, no, but seriously, it's fun if you know what you're expecting.
history.text: Look, at this point in this franchise, you already know what you're gonna get. You either like these movies or you don't. If you're expecting to suddenly start liking them, that's not gonna happen. On the flip side, I see a bunch of reviews from people who claim to have liked the previous ones but dislike this one. While not altogether an unlikely claim, the reasoning some people are giving is suspect, as this movie doesn't fail in ways the previous ones didn't. Everything you can claim this movie does bad was already present in the earlier entries, and sometimes it was even more blatant. I have a... complicated relationship with these movies. I understand they're bad (the first one being the only one I can legitimately call "decent"), I do not think they're "misunderstood", but I still like them. I still find enjoyment in watching them, for whatever reason I've never really bothered to dig up. Maybe I already know to go with low standards, maybe I find a deeper appreciation for the subtle storytelling that occurs way below the in-your-face loud screaming and explosions, maybe I just really like to see giant robots fight each other. It doesn't matter, the point is that I'm gonna review this film for what it is and not for what it should be because, again, at this point, it's what we have, and it's pointless to expect anything different as long as the same hands are in charge. And for what this movie franchise is, this is a pretty good entry in the series. The trailers would let you believe that the major plot of the movie is to have the Autobots fight a brainwashed Optimus Prime. In reality, that barely qualifies as a C-plot and it ends almost as soon as it starts. A bit dissapointing but not entirely unexpected. The real plot of the film is that the Decepticons are hunting for an old Transformer relic that will help them revive their old planet, Cybertron while, of course, the Autobots are trying to prevent it with the help of a group of humans who've been secretly working with Transformers for centuries. Meanwhile, tensions between humans and Transformers haven't really improved much since the events of the previous film (which, for a series that doesn't really do much in the way of continuity, surprisingly makes a lot of sense). At the other side of the universe, the alien creature responsible for the creation of Cybertron has brainwashed Optimus Prime and sends him in search of the relic. All of this culminates in a race against time in order to find and destroy the relic before Cybertron is fixed by sacrificing Earth (very much like in the events of the third film). So yeah, that's the plot. Nothing original and the climax is perhaps too similar to that of Dark of the Moon, but it's serviceable. The plot retcons events and ideas from the previous films here and there but that's nothing new. Acting is decent and visuals range from spectacular to "I have no idea what's going on", and dialogue ranges from "Oh, that's neat" to "Please, for the love of God, shut your mouth and never, ever open it again", so nothing new there either. Some truly emotional moments are underscored by preposterous writing that should entirely ruin them, but the performances are good enough that it doesn't, because the actors are putting the effort that the writers refuse to. Well, some of them anyway. There are more than a few continuity nods and gags about Transformers in other media, which should bring a smile to some people. In conclusion: it's a Michael Bay Transformers movie. Nothing more, nothing less. If you liked the previous ones, chances are you're gonna like this one. If you didn't like the previous ones, this one will do nothing to change your mind. While seen just as a movie this would earn a 1 and 1/2 star rating at most, as a Michael Bay Transformers movie it easily earns 4 stars.

history.title: Alien: Covenant
history.review_title: Watch only if you're interested in seeing Michael Fassbender making out with himself
history.text: Alien is a franchise made popular by its two first movies, which curiously belong to different genres. The first one is pretty much a horror film while the second one is action focused. Both of them are great and beloved for different reasons, showing that this is a franchise that works well in different approaches, even if the basic plot is similar. Unfortunately, later sequels have failed to take advantage of this and their quality has suffered due to poor writing. After a couple of crossovers with the Predator franchise, they decided to come back to basics making a prequel, Prometheus. Divisive as that film is, it does succeed of pulling the old trick by focusing on sci-fi this time. Alien: Covenant, a movie which is both a sequel to Prometheus and a prequel to the original Alien, unfortunately, can't decide what genre it wants to belong to. This is, sadly, the least of its problems. The movie suffers from terrible writing, terrible characterization and a complete lack of focus. The only reason this isn't the worst movie of the franchise is the existence of Alien vs Predator: Requiem. Though since that movie isn't considered canon, this one might as well take the title. The plot goes like this: a ship named The Covenant is traveling to a far world with the intention of colonizing a new planet. Out of sheer coincidence, they run into a distress signal, which they follow to a world that looks habitable for humans and decide to investigate. Proving that government-sanctioned employees are just as dumb and useless in the future as they are today, they explore the place unprotected, leading to a couple of them becoming infected by parasites that explode out of their bodies into Neomorphs (the precursors to Xenomorphs), who give them chase to a point where they're rescued by David, the android from Prometheus. He then proceeds to experiment with them in the guise of helping them in order to perfect the Xenomorph species, finally answering the question that literally no one was asking, Ridley Scott: how did the Aliens came to be? Here's the major problem with this film: it takes everything that's bad about all the previous ones and almost nothing that's good. The descent into cheap horror cliches from Resurrection and Requiem? It's here. The mentally challenged crew from Prometheus? It's here. The complete lack of tension from AvP? It's here. The lack of characterization from almost every movie after Alien 3? It's here. The excess CGI that has plagued the series since the third film, making some of the creatures painfully un-scary? It's here. Wanna know what's NOT here? Everything the end of Prometheus hinted at. Rather than building onto what that film ended on, they decided to just shove that aside and follow an entirely different path, effectively making Prometheus entirely pointless, which is a shame, because despite its problems (some of them very serious), it's a far superior film to this one. In the process of trying to fix the issues with that film they created a far worse one in almost every aspect. The few positives are as such: the movie looks beautiful, mostly. Leaving aside some grating CGI here and there, the visuals are gorgeous. Acting is mostly good, with Michael Fassbender being the clear standout, particularly considering he's playing two characters this time. And, I don't know, I guess I should give them props for the fact that Ridley Scott didn't come into my house to personally use my Blu-Ray collection of Alien movies as toilet paper. As a sci-fi, horror or action film this completely and utterly fails. As an Alien movie, it's frankly insulting. I can only recommend it to the most die-hard Michael Fassbender fans. Everyone else avoid even if you have to kiss a facehugger to do so.

No spoilers. Star Wars was at a crossroads after the divisive "Episode VII: The Force Awakens". That movie was a hit, but it was also accused of being too similar to "A New Hope", and rightly so, since it did rehashed many of that film's story beats and ideas. But, ultimately, it was understandable, as after the unpopularity of the prequels Disney decided to play it safe with the start of their new trilogy, and at least people were looking out to the next films expanding upon the new ideas and mysteries set by TFA. So now they needed to make a decision. Will the next movie play it safe too or take risks? After watching it, it seems they tried to do both, and they stumbled. "The Last Jedi" will probably end up being even more divisive than the previous film. This movie does not follow the same beats of the equivalent "The Empire Strikes Back", but it does take cues and similar ideas from other Star Wars movies, particularly "Return of the Jedi". But, in general, it does try new stuff, and it pays off in the sense that it feels original, but not in the sense that it feels unsatisfying. Ideas range from "Interesting" to "Why? Why in the world would you do that?" and story beats go from shocking to predictable. While TFA was directed by J. J. Abrams, TLJ is directed by Rian Johnson, and this man seems to take his job as a new president who's dead set in erasing away all the changes done by the previous administrations, whether those were good or bad. If you were excited for all of those ideas and mysteries TFA left, prepare to be dissapointed as literally every one of them gets changed, destroyed or outright ignored. If you were the kind of fan who got a kick of making theories about what could happen, prepare to throw those theories to the Sarlacc Pit. Yes, you'll most likely be surprised, but that doesn't mean it'll be in a good way. Most of the time it's better to be predictable than dissapointing. The most noticeable thing is that this movie doesn't really feel that much like Star Wars. Leaving aside Rey's personal subplots with Luke Skywalker and Kylo Ren, the rest of the film feels more inspired by Star Wars than an actual part of it. The stakes are there, but the scale isn't. There are a few interesting visuals in one of the (very) few planets visited, but that's it. This is particularly noticeable in Finn's subplot, which looks like it belongs to an entirely different film. There are a couple of new characters, none of which are even remotely interesting, and some of the older ones suffer from bad characterization. The ones coming from TFA are properly treated, though, particularly Rey and Kylo Ren, who get more fleshed out and oughta get more fans on their side because of it. There's also a cameo by a popular character that's neat to see and will probably bring a smile to your face, but it's unnecessary and frankly counterproductive to another character's development. A couple new creatures show up as well, and they're nothing interesting. If you were excited about porgs, I'll warn you that calling them a footnote in this film is doing them a favor. Visually speaking, this film is absolutely gorgeous, so it has that going for it. The score is as good as always, but nothing new stands out. All in all, it's an entertaining film, but only an average Star Wars movie. Unlike Rogue One, it has characters you care about. Unlike TFA, it has an original storyline. Unlike the prequels, it's not saddled with complicated politics and silly visuals. But in trying to avoid those old pitfalls it runs into entirely different ones. I recommend not to watch any previous Star Wars films right before seeing this movie, since you're more likely to appreciate it if you don't have the previous ones in mind. Unless, of course, you never watched them, in which case it's absolutely necessary.

history.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past (The Rogue Cut)
history.review_title: The best version of this film, but not a must-have
history.text: X-Men: Days of Future Past is one of the best comic book movies in existence. It has great action, tension, characterization, a well-crafted and perfectly paced storyline and amazing visuals and scoring. I was a bit scared for this cut, since I felt it might ruin the film's pacing, but luckily, my fears didn't pan out. This is the definitive version of the film. That being said, it is only ever so slightly, so unless you're a completionist or really curious, if you already have the theatrical version of the film, this one is practically unnecessary. The plot of the film isn't changed, but the extra scenes add some interesting bits of story and characterization that fit the tone of the film and help the movie feel more cohesive. They also address a couple of minimal plot holes from the original, though sadly they still don't bother to explain stuff that left casual audiences confused, such as Professor Xavier's return after his death in X-Men III (which was addressed elsewhere) and Kitty Pride's new, unexplained consciousness-time-travel powers (which were never addressed). There are also a couple of new extras that are far more interesting that the ones included in the original version, so that's definitely a plus. The one thing that puzzles me, though, is the decision to call this extended edition "The Rogue Cut". Yeah, Rogue is there now, but her screen time is absolutely minimal and her role in the film ends up largely unjustified (she's supposed to be there to replace Kitty Pride after she's injured, but the movie never makes it look necessary by, saying, having Kitty die from her injuries at some point later). So yeah, if you don't already own any version of the movie, this is the one to go, but if you do own the theatrical version it's certainly not a priority.

history.title: Justice League: Throne of Atlantis (Blu-ray)
history.text: "Justice League: Throne of Atlantis" is the sequel to "Justice League: War", the third DC DTV movie from the New 52-based films kickstarted by "The Flashpoint Paradox". After DC rebooted their comics universe with their New 52 imprint they decided to do the same with their animated movies. The reception has been more or less the same in both media: lukewarm but still managing to attract a lot of audience. Regarding quality, it's generally mediocre, and this is no exception. This is the consequence of having this new series of films being directly adapted from stories from the comics rather than merely inspired by them, and the comics are generally mediocre. While I haven't read the comic this movie is based on, I've read other Aquaman comics from the New 52 imprint, and it's apparent that this movie doesn't do the characters any favors. The storyline for this movie is a largely watered-down version of the Justice League episode "The Enemy Below". While there's gore here where there wasn't in the animated series, characterization is far weaker, which is a bad thing, considering the basic plot (man tries to kill family to inherit the throne and do as he pleases with the kingdom) is extremely derivative. The Justice League episode made up for that with amazing character arcs and fun action, but this movie lacks in both departments. Most characters feel like caricatures of their originals, if not outright useless. In fact, Aquaman pretty much feels like less than a secondary character in what's arguably his own movie. The story also suffers from bad pacing, having most of the running time dedicated to setup and things only really starting to move along way past the halfway point, then ending abruptly. Then there are the subplots, which are just as weak. There's the bit about the Justice League not being sure if they're an actual team or not, which is mentioned once and never again brought up. The same happens with Batman's reluctance to be part of the group, which last about ten seconds. There's still the romance between Superman and Wonder Woman that no fan in history was ever invested in. There's even an eliminated sequence seen on the extras regarding Batman's investigation on Scarecrow. The sequence is short (less than a minute), but feels entirely pointless and it would have ruined the pacing of the film even further if included. Speaking of extras, these are definitely the highlight of the disc. There are a few features on DC underwater villains, a Comic Con panel, the film's score and, as usual, four included episodes from DC's cartoons, all of them associated to Aquaman, and all of them far more fun and interesting than the movie. So, if you're a completionist, go for it when it's cheap. Otherwise, avoid. It does nothing new or interesting and your time is best spent watching something else.

history.title: Starship Troopers 4K UHD
history.review_title: the best this movie has ever looked
history.text: Starship Troopers has not aged very well. Too much blood and guts with a little Nazism thrown in and some gratuitous nudity. It came across as ground-breaking in its special effects back in the day. Today, it's just another rather pointless actioner with a lot of taut flesh thrown to the slaughter or Ginsu-ed by some horrendous CGI bugs. Yuck! The 4K presentation is, of course, the best this movie has ever looked. But with so many better movies in Sony's Columbia/Tri-Star cannon, why did this one get pushed to the front of the line. How about The Remains of the Day, Little Women, Sense and Sensibility, Annie, A Man for All Seasons, Tootsie, Steel Magnolias...the list could go on and on. Bottom line: ultra-violent to the point of anesthetizing, Starship Troopers is not the movie you remember it to be. The disc is perfect. The movie...anything but.

history.title: They Shoot Horses, Don t They? (Special Edition) [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: This isn't a feel good but a 'whoa
history.text: Darkly disturbing and poignantly acted, They Shoot Horses Don't They is given a royal release on Blu-ray and it is about time. Too many surprises along the way, but suffice it to say, Jane Fonda is doing some stellar acting here, along with Bruce Dern and Red Buttons. The 1080p transfer looks marvelous. Just buy it and prepare to be shocked by what you see. This isn't a feel good but a 'whoa...how on earth did something like this get made in the first place?' Great movie making like this was rare back then. Today, it's all but nonexistent. Regrets there.

history.title: Since You Went Away (Roadshow Edition)
history.review_title: A great cast and an important story to tell
history.text: Since You Went Away is the sort of wartime weepy that deserves far more recognition than it has received in the years since WWII. A great cast and an important story to tell. Kino's Blu-ray is a mess; riddled in artifacts, noise, a barrage of age-related damage. Why this release was not given the necessary clean up it deserves is beyond me. Buy for content. The disc will definitely not win any awards!

history.title: Suspect - 30th Anniversary - Blu-ray
history.review_title: Suspect has Cher's mesmerizing performance to recommend it. It's not enough to save the film
history.text: Cliched and silly, Suspect has Cher's mesmerizing performance to recommend it. It's not enough to save the film, but it yields some fairly solid scenes between her and co-stars, Liam Neeson and Dennis Quaid. The plot starts off solid but then devolves into dreck. By the end you'll be left saying "oh please" - words, effectively to describe any Blu-ray marked as a 30th anniversary edition that offer virtually no extra features and a 1080p transfer that is only marginally appealing. Bottom line: Suspect is highly suspect as an entertainment. Cher gets top marks. But even she cannot save this turkey.

history.title: Lost Horizon
history.review_title: Even the less than perfect 16mm inserts look exceptionally clean
history.text: Frank Capra's towering achievement gets a royal Blu-ray release from Sony, restoring a minute and a half to a movie that, regrettably is still piece work of the original release. Will other materials resurface in years to come. We hope so. What's here has been given utmost consideration by Sony. Even the less than perfect 16mm inserts look exceptionally clean, with image stabilization applied. This is a classic beyond most and deserves top shelf consideration in any collector's collection. Buy today. Treasure forever.

history.title: Brigadoon [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Lerner and Loewe's melodic masterpiece looks almost perfect on Blu-ray
history.text: Lerner and Loewe's melodic masterpiece looks almost perfect on Blu-ray. WAC has done a lot to preserve the flawed AnscoColor. We give them top marks. This transfer looks a little weak in its saturation, also its contrast. The story is timeless; two pals from the jaded present stumbling across a mythical Scottish village that materializes once every hundred years from the highland mists. Gene Kelly and Cyd Charisse dance to perfection. Van Johnson is sublime as the cynical best friend. Great performances and a superb score, regrettably missing one of my favorite songs, "Come to Me, Bend to Me" filmed but cut from the final release. It's here as an extra. Were that it belonged to the film proper. Oh well, it never did. What's here is going to impress. Prepare for a delightful night at the movies.

history.review_title: Disgusting that Fox should reissue its severely flawed Blu-ray from ...
history.text: Disgusting that Fox should reissue its severely flawed Blu-ray from a decade ago with different cover art but the same digital anomalies afflicting this disc. The image is too dark and riddled in heavy-handed DNR and edge enhancement. If you already own Miracle on 34th Street on Blu-ray there is NO GOOD REASON to repurchase it here. Skip and send a message to Fox. A new transfer is in order for something claiming to be a 70th anniversary! Bah, humbug!

history.review_title: A Very Good Old New Film Expirence
history.text: I decided to view my VHS – 4 box collection of the 'Alien Quadrology: Alien, Aliens, Aliens 3, and Alien Resurrection', with Sigourney Weaver (an outstanding actress, but not in 'Avatar' the movie) . My newly installed and digital sound system picked up every flaw that those VHS reals could provide, it was so bad in sound quality, that I immediately turned it off – it was to much to endure – and the projected picture from VHS on wide screen television was like looking threw a frosted lens – I immediately as an audience said, 'cut!'. However, when I ordered from Amazon.com the 'Aliens Quadrilogy on DVD, the weather on my contemporary sound and visual system had completely cleared, and to my absolute surprise, the DVD of the four Aliens Quidrilogy included the scenes that where cut from the theatrical version of the movies ( which is something that needs to happen with Russell Crows acting production of the 'Gladiators'). For several hours I watched everyone of the Aliens Quidrilogy, as if I was watching an entirely new movie – oddly enough it was a new movie – it was a horrifying but beautiful experience in film audience participation which really did surprise me. I did this in particular, because there is a new version of Aliens to be released soon for movie fanatics like myself – I will be in the theater for sure with this new release of Aliens, I recommend a review of the old productions of Aliens before attending the new release, but please, only on DVD digital visual and sound devices.

history.title: The Hot Chick
history.review_title: The Obvious Mirth Got Lost In Social Mythology
history.text: The Hot Chick movie, was a little disappointing for me, maybe because I am a homosexual, and would have gone in a more adult direction, that made a real social psychological statement about being ‘unashamed of being gay and transgender, and maybe realizing that you need to come out, because heterosexuality wasn’t your real cup of tea anymore’. The film had an excellent flow in editing idea, plot, and what I like to call film movement, but I think the film was made to appeal to heterosexual audiences mythology of how gay or transgender people are expected to act in heterosexuals minds and eye. The film could have been both funny but yet a serious comedy that made a statement, but yet lost non of its expected and obvious mirth, which the director did not take advantage of as a film.

history.text: Bringing Down The House, as a film, is one of those film that was a good idea, but then got lost in African American social mythology and stereo types. What would be so wrong with making a film that remained a comedy, but yet this African American woman who meant a Caucasian man and they fell madly in love with one another, to the point where true love can so often do, really change both they’re lives for the better, whatever better may be considered for people genuinely in love. The film obviously avoided the reality that an interracial couple can be in love, and become a family. Our own president Barrack O’Bama mother certainly proved that people fall in love, and cares little about racial differences, and trying to conform to your movie audience, and audiences inability to accept an interracial couple being in love: and this film, in places, when its not conforming to its audience, has a great deal of mirth and great plot, and well acted.

There’s parts in this Introducing Dorothy Dandridge Film with Halle Berry that does exactly that, and even though Halle Berry is a very talented woman, I sometime capture a little distance in her character in this film, like she was doing the best she could under the circumstances, and then in other scene in this film, she was totally in character – till I forgot just how beautiful Halle Berry is or was, people change over the years, and I have not seen her in a good role for a long time. history.title: Philomena
history.text: This movie deserves Oscar all star winner. It was just nominated 4 awards. Philomena(Judi Dench) is the name of the English woman who was grown in a convent by nuns. When she was 16, she got pregnant and the nuns treated her as a sinner, took away her child, sold him to America. After 50 years, she is desperate to find her adopted son and her daugher meets this journalist (Steve Googan) who usually writes other matters rather than human stories but finally decides to help her finding her son/ write a story about what happened back then. There are severel or many of the same or similar stories already made from Europe but none of them touched me this deep. Only Stephen Frears –FLORENCE Foster JENKINS, THE QUEEN, MRS HENDERSON PRESENT- can be possible made this emotionally so touching drama. Also Judi Dench once and for all deserves an Oscar winner for sure. She was not flamboyant or cried or shout or anything but she was so very herself all into the character. I was even wanted to see this movie a little more even during the credit is rolling. I wanted to see more of her life! Philomena’s life! All of the Stephen Frears’ movies are so delicate and instant classic that you should just have to buy them and collect them. Steve Googan doesn’t believe in god that much. He thinks that they are in some way fraud. When he hears about what happened to Judi Dench, he was so angry and that anger helped her all the way. I felt his justice. When they finally have researched and even meets the lover of the son, they found out that after the son- he was gay and got AIDS- got AIDS, he visited the convent to trace his mother, they all lied by saying she abandoned him and never wanted to meet him. He was even buried in the yard at the convent. They thought that she was a sinner and deserved not to even meet the son even after 50 years apart. May I ask what kind of a sin that she’ve made? Had sex with a boy whom he loved at an early age? Is that it? Is is so against god that she has to let go of him abroad not even knowing that the nuns are selling the baby to America? Not even be able to meet him after he was succeeded –He became a team for the President Regan as a politician– and came back to meet her but they lied that she didn’t wanted to see him ever? Sometimes if the movie is so real, the charactors are so great, as an audience, I become so angry as well at the fact. But how she reacted was, I was wrong. I am happy to know that I finally had a chance to retrace him. Don’t blame the nuns. They did nothing wrong. I was wrong. But for Steve Googan as a man, he couldn’t help becoming so angry. The very old nun still think that she is a sinner and what she did was all right. After everything have been passed, they finally wrote this into a book. It was all revealed into this book. As I said, there are a lot of similar movies dealing with this matter but this movie stands alone so vivid because of the director Stephen Frears. He knows how to cook two actors so well. Judi Dench constantly talks about what she thinks, at the beginning it was kind of tiresome but as time goes by we begin to fall in love with that. Steve Googan, a kind understanding man, a man with responsibility, brave and righteous man. This movie deserves more attention. history.title: Father Brown: Season Three, Part Two
history.review_title: Another Season (or 1/2) of a Great Mystery with Humor from England
history.text: This is a continuation of the best presentation (video) of the Father Brown stories with a superb cast that leaves the audience feeling they really are the people they are playing. Other than Mark Williams, my favorite is Nancy Carroll who plays the Baroness of the area. She's a hoot and ends up doing things she would never have dreamed of doing like getting her Chanel dirty, all with a very dry wit. The writing is very well written, and in this set unlike those with Kenneth More of the 1970's in the role of Father Brown, John Light plays Hercule Flambeau when he is still a rogue rather than after his reformation which makes for a nice difference between the two series. Thankfully, this series is being made at least through 2017 and hopefully for even longer. Nothing against Kenneth More, this production is better produced, better acted, more lively, and just plain great as most English series are today. Were it not for English productions put to DVD, or shown on DVD our TV and DVD player sales would plummet.

history.title: Masterpiece Mystery!: Inspector Lewis 8 (Full UK-Length Edition) (Blu-ray)
history.review_title: The Climax Season of a Great Series--unusual for a spin-off series. Thank you, England for More Great TV.
history.text: This is the climex of one of the best Copper shows to come out of England and as a spin-off from another great for its time, Inspector Morse. In the series, it was satisfying that Lewis accepted Hathaway, or vice versa as it were, and equally so that he learned who killed his wife. It was interesting to learn why Hathaway became a cop and left the Catholic ministry (pre-seminary at Cambridge). Throughout the series, poor Lewis, with a consolidated school education through high school, learned his skills the hard way, with Morse being worn down by Morse his boss, always correcting his grammar, and who attended Oxford, and then Lewis his Sergeant, quoting to him Shakespeare or some other poet or writer or philosopher, below him and educated at Cambridge. But, he took it as he had to and learned to get it right. And learn, he did. It was a great run for Kevin Whately, from the mid 80's to the mid teens in a new century, about 30 years and his early role in Miss Marple A Murder is Announced playing a cop guarding the door of the home of the murderer. A lot of copping for Whately.

However, to Murdoch, he considers his lowly title really "in name" only. Unless I was dreaming, this was the only season that did not leave us hanging on a Hitchcockian 'top of Mount Rushmore', or on the 'top of the Statue of Liberty' before the last salvo of being saved. Sadly, there was no season ending cliffhanger leaving us with baited breath. Other than that, we have lost the beautiful medical examiner (Coroner) to her 'new' LGBT lifestyle. The other Mystery were typical Murdoch.

history.title: Agatha Christie's Poirot: Complete Case Collection
history.review_title: SHAME ON ACORN FOR SUCH LAZINESS
history.text: Of course the Suchet performances are 10-star, par-excellence, will never be repeated to this level; but I wish to rate this one-star only because of the mix in sound. This set has so many various sound outputs; i.e. PCM, Dolby and DTS. Why not make all discs in all three audio formats and allow the user the option to choose which one to use. In my particular case, my audio output is a Bose Solo and anything Bose (almost anything) will not support DTS or Dolby Atmos or TrueHD only Dolby 5.1. When there is no option as the later discs in this set which are many as are the latest output of another long running English murder mystery series running beginning in 1997 and since switching to Blu-Ray in the past few years, I have to switch over to my horrible internal TV speakers. Bose simply will not support high-end Dolby or more frustratingly DTS of any type. So, Acorn, how much trouble would it have been, as do most movies, have a setup option, and allow us to decide which audio format we would like to hear it under? Thankfully, another reviewer went to the trouble to detail which discs had which type of audio for which I am eternally grateful. I won’t make this purchase which would be quite expensive especially since I have all the DVDs already.

history.title: Ruth Rendell Mysteries Collection
history.text: The real problem with this series and any other regarding Ruth Rendell is that Acorn or any other has not put any Wexford Mysteries except for three: Road Rage, Simisola, and Harm Done—the last three Inspector Wexford Mysteries that were filmed. And from what Acorn told me, there are no plans for the remaining Wexford mysteries to be put to DVD much less to BVD. At least not any time soon. My guess is that Acorn does not believe that the demand across the pond and in the US would not be high enough to cover the cost of paying royalties, etc.

history.title: Tudors: The Complete Series
history.review_title: A peak at British history...with American accents
history.text: The issues I had with the series are - That for a British story, hardly anyone spoke with a British accent - The dialogue uses modern phrases and words that were not used in that time period For example: A young woman says to a man "You're weird." - There are numerous sex scenes within the first 30 minutes - 4 or 5, and very little story. Plus, some of the words used during these types of scenes are modern slang/swear words - It's historically in accurate. Some one commits suicide by slitting his own throat. But in actual history, he died from natural causes. - In reality, Henry had reddish hair. In this story, he starts out as a blonde, but by epiosode 3 of the second season, his hair is jet black. Although the sets appear accurate, the clothing does not. The clothing doesn't seem correct for the time period, and looks cheap and held together by paste in some scenes. It is almost like the clothes were rented out from a costume shop. And who wore hairstyles like that if this time period? NO ONE! If you're looking for a drama, it is ok. But if you're looking for accuracy, this production has major flaws.

history.title: The Boy (2016)
history.review_title: Not as thrilling as the trailer implies...
history.text: It has all been done before, and much better. The story idea was a good idea, but somehow loses all suspense here. The only jolts you'll get are from sudden loud music or a bang. And that will only happen if you're still awake. If I give the titles of the movies this reminds me of, then I would be giving the "twist" away to those who may love this unimaginative film. I think that is what turned me off the most about this film. That there is no originality about it. And there is no real suspense built.

history.title: Upstairs, Downstairs
history.text: A person really shouldn't compare this to the original series, but it's pretty hard not to. There is no comparison to it. The original had a low budget, but it had compelling stories and a lovable cast. Who could forget Ruby, the kitchen maid. She barley had many lines, but she managed to steal almost every scene she played. The set was small, but the characters were awesome. Jump ahead to this "reboot" of sorts. Gone are all of the original characters except for Rose. It was wonderful to see her, but that was the only thing good about this series this time. As for the other characters, who cares? All cardboard, all dull, in a slow moving, unexciting story. The new kitchen maid Ivy was grating. Always carrying on about something and terrible to understand. The set itself, even though in the extras it was stated it was built off of the original, is by far the worst "copy" ever. It's huge! And nothing like the old set. My advice? Skip this one. There's better series to watch out there.

history.title: The Returned [DVD + Digital]
history.text: It's the Hollywood version and not as compelling as the French version. I remember the ending of "Pee-Wee's Big Adventure". Hollywood wanted to make Pee-Wee's story and fluffed the story up to where it was almost unrecognizable. It was hilarious. Well, that's what happened here and it isn't as good as the French original version. The American producers missed the foreboding atmosphere of the French version. They also missed the tension the French version builds. If you can stand subtitles, watch the French version instead.

history.title: Penny Dreadful: The Final Season
history.text: I was disappointed in the final season. The acting, production, and music were top notch. The writing was, to be honest, awful. The writers didn't seem to understand the existing characters at all. For example, in season 2. Hecate was a powerful witch. But by season 3, she hardly had any magic in her at all. The stories were not linked together at all. In previous seasons, the stories were linked and then resolved at the end. Season 3's stories were, for the most part, ridiculous. Lily's revenge army was ludicrous. There are almost full episodes of the characters self absorbed soul searching with endless, whining dialogue. It would have been ok if what they were saying was interesting, but it wasn't. It was dull. By the time the final episode rolled around, it was evident the writers had no clue about the characters. Instead, it was written like a pale imitation of a super hero movie or the Matrix with choreographed fight scenes. How could 5 people kill hundreds of vampires and at least not one or two of the five get killed?

history.text: The first half of the season was excellent. But then the story changed directions and wasn't so good. The first part was chilling and actually scary in parts without being gory, but the second half chose the slasher route. ugh. Another setback is the over use of Sara Paulson as a lead again. She's a great actress, but is over used in this series. In the extras, a number of the cast participate on a panel. Sara was on this panel and was completely rude. She kept manhandling the other stars, especially Kathy Bates. Sara kept putting her hand over Kathy's mouth whenever she tried to speak. Finally, Kathy just told her to shut up.
